title: N-D-V

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-N-H: the soft answer, the poor one who is heard, and Moses, very meek. Your line was answer humbly. Today, a gift nobody can require.

Here is a fundraiser that had to be shut down for raising too much. The people in the wilderness are building the mishkan, the sanctuary, and they keep bringing gold, silver, yarn, linen, wood, every morning, more. Finally the craftsmen go to Moses and say: "The people bring much more than enough." So Moses has it announced through the camp: stop. And the scene ends with a line that's almost funny: "So the people were restrained from bringing." Restrained. From giving.

segments.voice: N-D-V. Nun, dalet, vet. Nedavah: a freewill gift, a voluntary offering. The verb: to give of your own accord, to volunteer. First, the instruction. When God asks for gifts for the sanctuary, the request is left open: "of every man that giveth it willingly with his heart ye shall take my offering." The gift is measured by the heart that moves it, not the size. And the text calls what they bring a nedavah, from men and women whose hearts made them willing. Second, the person. From the same letters comes nadiv: a generous person, and also a noble one. Isaiah says: "the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand." In that old English, liberal means generous, and the Hebrew is nadiv. Notice the verb: deviseth. The generous person plans generosity, thinks it up, the way someone else plans a business. Third, the difference. Jewish law also has required giving. Tzedakah, the giving to the poor, is commanded; the Torah's tithes are counted. A nedavah is the gift nobody can require. Both matter, and neither replaces the other. But the nedavah has its own shine: the people heard the request and simply kept coming, until someone had to ask them to stop. A free gift isn't free because it costs nothing. It's free because nobody made you.

segments.voice: Think of something you could give that nobody has asked for or expects, time, a skill, a meal, a compliment you've held back, a note to a teacher from years ago, and let a few ideas come. Choose one, notice how it feels to choose it freely, and devise it the way Isaiah's generous person does: when, where, how. If you pray, you can offer it in your prayer.

segments.voice: N-D-V. Nun, dalet, vet: the root of nedavah, the freewill gift, and nadiv, the generous one. Today's word.
Your line: free gift. The best ones are planned with care, and never required. That's day one thousand four hundred ten.

howItsDone: Alongside obligatory tzedakah, Jewish tradition honors the nedavah, a gift given of one's own accord; the wilderness sanctuary in Exodus was built from such freewill offerings.
